walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme B: Religion & Life — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme B: Religion & Life brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme B: Religion & Life.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Jesus was half God and half human.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
